facts.claim: Barry Marshall drank a Helicobacter pylori culture in July 1984 and developed gastritis after the exposure.
facts.mechanism: Because the self-experiment connected the bacterium to a resulting gastric inflammation in a previously healthy host, it challenged the view that such organisms were harmless passengers.
facts.commonError: Marshall won acceptance by presenting only an expert title and never exposing himself to the bacterium.
facts.whyWrong: The unusually memorable credential was the documented self-experiment, not professional status by itself.

facts.claim: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren received the 2005 Nobel Prize for the discovery of Helicobacter pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.
facts.mechanism: Because their work established a bacterial cause, ulcer treatment could target infection rather than treating acid alone.
facts.commonError: The Nobel recognition established that every stomach symptom is caused by Helicobacter pylori.
facts.whyWrong: The award concerns the bacterium's causal role in specified gastric diseases, not a universal explanation for all symptoms.

facts.claim: Pam Laffin developed emphysema at age 24 and had a lung removed before appearing in antismoking media.
facts.mechanism: Because her body and family bore visible costs of smoking, her warning had experience-based relevance that a detached endorsement lacked.
facts.commonError: Laffin was a healthy celebrity hired to recite a generic public-health script.
facts.whyWrong: She appeared as a patient and mother living with severe smoking-related disease, which is the basis of the antiauthority credential.

facts.claim: The Beyond War demonstration used 1 BB as the Hiroshima reference and thousands of BBs to represent the larger nuclear arsenal.
facts.mechanism: Because listeners could hear the contrast between a single impact and a prolonged cascade, the ratio became perceptible rather than remaining an abstract count.
facts.commonError: The BB demonstration replaced quantitative comparison with an unrelated scary noise.
facts.whyWrong: Each BB represented a consistent unit, so the sound preserved the scale relationship while translating it.

facts.claim: On October 28, 1980, Ronald Reagan asked debate viewers whether they were better off than four years earlier.
facts.mechanism: Because each voter could compare present conditions with personal memory, the question outsourced part of the credibility test to the audience.
facts.commonError: The line asked viewers to trust Reagan's private economic calculations without consulting their lives.
facts.whyWrong: Its persuasive design points listeners toward their own comparison rather than an inaccessible calculation.

facts.claim: Safexpress's 2007 Harry Potter launch assignment involved an Indian first stock of about 240,000 copies.
facts.mechanism: Because a secretive, simultaneous, high-volume launch imposes demanding logistics constraints, successful execution serves as relevant proof for later distribution claims.
facts.commonError: A Sinatra Test is an unrelated famous client name that proves every possible capability.
facts.whyWrong: The prior performance must be difficult and relevant to the new claim; fame without task fit is weak evidence.

facts.claim: An antiauthority derives credibility from direct, costly experience rather than conventional prestige.
facts.mechanism: Because the source has borne the consequence under discussion, audiences can treat the testimony as relevant evidence rather than remote promotion.
facts.commonError: An antiauthority is simply an uninformed person chosen because experts are always untrustworthy.
facts.whyWrong: The source is persuasive only when lived experience creates special access to the claim's consequences.

facts.claim: The human-scale principle translates a statistic into a familiar comparison while preserving the original relationship.
facts.mechanism: Because working memory can simulate everyday units more readily than huge totals, the audience can grasp magnitude without discarding quantity.
facts.commonError: Human-scaling permits changing the ratio as long as the resulting image feels dramatic.
facts.whyWrong: A distorted comparison sacrifices truth; the translation must retain the quantitative structure it explains.

facts.claim: A testable credential lets the audience verify a claim through an accessible observation or comparison.
facts.mechanism: Because the listener can perform the check independently, belief no longer rests entirely on the communicator's asserted authority.
facts.commonError: A testable credential is a promise that only the speaker can evaluate using private data.
facts.whyWrong: Private evidence cannot be audience-tested and therefore leaves the original trust problem intact.
